newsitem.title: PERU: Latam labor outlook poor despite growth - U.N..
newsitem.headline: Latam labor outlook poor despite growth - U.N..

text.p: Despite healthy overall economic growth throughout Latin American and the Caribbean in 1996, the region's labor situation made no progress, the United Nation's International Labor Organization (ILO) said Friday.

An ILO report issued from its regional headquarters in Peru said this year's average three percent economic growth in Latin America and the Caribbean had failed to prevent the unemployment rate rising to eight percent.

"On the one hand, the Latin American economy was able to overcome the crisis of 1995," the report said. "But in contrast the unemployment rate continued its upward tendency, reaching its highest level since the crisis of the mid-1980s."
The report did not give comparative jobless levels for the region in 1995, but said the figure was 6.0 percent in 1993.
"The problem of youth unemployment is worsening, even in countries where the overall rate of unemployment is falling, like Chile," it added.

The report added that 80 percent of new jobs in the region during 1996 were "low-quality," with poor wage and productivity levels. And industrial salaries fell 0.4 percent overall in real terms during the year.
"The message that seems to be emerging is that growth continues to be insufficient to improve the situation of employment and salaries," the report said.

Employment actually increased throughout the region at an average 2.6 percent, but this was opaqued by a 3.2 percent rise in the population seeking work. However, the panorama varied starkly from nation to nation.
The ILO singled out Chile and Paraguay for their "high- quality" performance in the labor sphere, combining a reduction in unemployment, improvement in job quality and a growth in salaries.

Seven countries registered a "deterioration" in their labor situation -- Mexico, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Panama, Bolivia, Jamaica and Venezuela. And seven showed "an intermediate situation where progress in some indicators was compensated by deterioration in others" -- Brazil, Barbados, Argentina, Colombia, Peru, Trinidad and Tabago, and Uruguay.

Finally, the report highlighted the plight of the region's 18 million child-workers, "many of them in risky conditions and most with restricted possibilities of human development and future labor prospects."
